stories.headline: Trump promises an AI czar and an AI Force, and rejects new guardrails
stories.standfirst: The president called safety concerns a hoax on Saturday, days after laboratory chiefs urged a slower pace, and the industry says it does not know what the force would do.
body: President Trump said on Saturday that he will appoint an official responsible for artificial intelligence and form what he called an AI Force, Reuters and the Washington Post reported. He gave no detail on either. Axios reported the force is modelled on Space Force. The Post said the announcement rejected calls from lawmakers and industry leaders for new guardrails.

The statement came as parts of the industry ask for a slower pace. Bloomberg reported that Trump continued to push companies to race ahead with development despite growing fears about safety, and TechCrunch reported that he claimed, without evidence, that the backlash against AI is a Democratic hoax. The Wall Street Journal called it his first call for federal oversight of the industry.

Reaction was muted. Politico reported that the tech industry is scratching its head over the proposal. CNBC reported on Sunday that Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has emerged as the president's closest ally in the debate. Trump telephoned Huang on stage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday, CNBC said, to tell him the robots are not going to take over the world.

Opposition is growing among voters, according to the Journal. WIRED reported on Sunday that the president's base is running the opposite way on data centres. CNBC said that AI and data centre alarms were the main topic at the Congressional Black Caucus's annual gathering in Washington this week, on both sides of the argument.

Nothing has been filed. The BBC, the FT and the Hill reported the plan with no name for the czar and no date for the force. What it would do, who would staff it, and whether it needs an act of Congress are questions none of the accounts answers.

stories.headline: Subscribers sue Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Google over the AI slowdown
stories.standfirst: The complaint, reported by the AP, says Dario Amodei's 12 September essay amounted to an invitation to collude, and that a coordinated slowdown cuts the value of paid subscriptions.
body: A lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Google made an illegal agreement to slow the pace of their AI development, the Associated Press reported on Saturday. The plaintiffs are individual subscribers to AI services. They argue the companies violated antitrust law when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts. Doing so, they say, reduces the value consumers get for paid subscriptions.

The coordination largely took place on 12 September, the complaint argues. That is the day Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, published an essay urging industry-wide cooperation on decelerating advances in favour of safety measures, according to CBS News. A post circulating in Chinese says four consumers filed the case in the Northern District of California on 18 September. The AP account does not give that detail.

The suit arrives in a week when the argument over pace ran in both directions. Trump said on Saturday that his administration would not hinder or stifle the industry's growth. Reuters reported the same day that Anthropic is considering releasing a new model despite calling for a slowdown. The Information reported that investors say the calls to slow down are making some customers wary of buying AI products.

None of the four companies has responded publicly in the material we have seen. The complaint's central claim is that an essay and matching public statements amount to an agreement. That is a legal theory no court has ruled on. The AP account does not say what damages are sought, and the filing itself was not available to us.

stories.headline: Bessent and He open talks on AI and critical minerals in New York
stories.standfirst: The treasury secretary and China's vice premier meet on Sunday ahead of Xi Jinping's visit, with AI, trade and critical minerals on the agenda, Reuters reports.
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China's vice premier, He Lifeng, will launch talks on AI, trade and critical minerals, Reuters reported on Sunday. Bloomberg said on Saturday that the two would lead talks on trade and other pressure points in New York on Sunday. Reuters had earlier reported, citing a source, that Bessent planned to discuss AI and rare earths.

The meeting was set for 10.30am Eastern at JPMorgan's Manhattan headquarters, with the trade representative Jamieson Greer attending, according to a market summary posted on X, which also noted that the US-China trade truce expires on 10 November. Bloomberg's Sunday audio bulletins ran the talks alongside Hormuz shipments as the day's main stories.

The talks precede Xi Jinping's visit. The New York Post reported on Friday that Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk and Sam Altman have invitations to the White House state dinner for Xi. Other accounts list Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Sundar Pichai, Tim Cook and Michael Dell. One, citing NPR, says China asked for more than half of the roughly 100 seats for its own delegation.

AI is on the Trump-Xi agenda, according to an account citing senior US officials. What talks on AI mean at treasury level is not spelled out in any of the reports. Reuters has spent the week on distillation, the technique by which one lab trains on another's outputs, which it calls one of the most politically fraught questions in the standoff.

stories.headline: Big Tech keeps $300bn of AI exposure off its balance sheets, FT reports
stories.standfirst: Guarantees issued in under a year back debt for data centres and chips while recording little of the exposure, and Nvidia's backing of an OpenAI site is the largest cited.
body: Big Tech companies are rapidly expanding their use of guarantees to back debt for AI data centres and chips, the Financial Times reported on Sunday. They have issued up to $300bn in commitments in less than a year while recording little of that exposure on their balance sheets. The paper called it a new way for Wall Street to turn the companies' credit strength into cheaper funding.

Posts summarising the report give the components. Nvidia is guaranteeing up to $105bn behind OpenAI's Ohio data centre project, according to one such summary. Broadcom has up to $29bn of exposure tied to AI racks for Anthropic. Meta carries a residual-value guarantee of about $28bn tied to its Hyperion site. We have not seen the article itself.

The figures sit inside a larger estimate. One post reproducing an FT chart cites Morgan Stanley's estimate of $3.1tn in total off-balance-sheet commitments across the hyperscalers. Bloomberg published its own piece on Sunday describing AI's influence on markets and the US economy as a house of cards. Any spending slowdown may be devastating, it said.

The report follows the FT's account on Thursday of an OpenAI presentation projecting $856bn of compute and infrastructure spending and $278bn of negative free cash flow through 2030. A guarantee is not a loss, and none of the reports says any has been called. Replies to the report ask who takes the first loss if utilisation or pricing slips before the next refinancing.

stories.headline: Alibaba's Qwen releases a 7B image model with open weights
stories.standfirst: Qwen-Image-2.1 generates and edits in one model, takes up to ten reference images and outputs transparent layers, and ComfyUI and vLLM supported it within the hour.
body: Alibaba's Qwen team released Qwen-Image-2.1 on Sunday with open weights, describing it as a unified model for both generation and editing in a lightweight 7B package. The company says it natively generates and edits RGBA layers, supports up to 10 reference images with precise local control, and improves text rendering and portraits over its predecessor.

Third parties confirmed the release within the hour. ComfyUI said the model is supported, describing one 7B checkpoint that generates and edits, with image generation at native 2K and instruction editing from up to 10 reference images in a single pass. The vLLM project said it has day-0 support in vLLM-Omni, and put the architecture at a 7.1B diffusion transformer paired with Qwen3-VL-8B.

Qwen says the model outperforms most closed-source models and that inference on multi-image inputs is drastically accelerated. Those are the company's claims, and no independent benchmark has appeared. Local edits can be specified by circling regions, according to Qwen's examples, which show a watch removed, hair recoloured and clothing replaced in one pass.

The licence is the caveat. One developer who read it on Hugging Face describes it as strictly non-commercial, with no revenue cap. That would limit the model to research and personal use unless Alibaba grants separate terms, a point the launch thread does not address. The team had trailed the release ten hours earlier with a one-line post.

stories.headline: StepFun launches Step 5 Preview, with open weights due on 15 October
stories.standfirst: The Chinese lab's flagship is a 600B-parameter mixture of experts activating 27B per token, with a million-token context and pricing of $1 per million input tokens.
body: StepFun introduced Step 5 Preview on Sunday as its new flagship model for agentic work. It claims frontier-level performance across software engineering and professional knowledge work, with particular strength in finance. The company says it is a 600B total, 27B active mixture-of-experts model with a 1M-token context and vision. It is available now through the API, and open weights are to follow on 15 October.

Figures circulating from the model page put input at $1 per million tokens and output at $2.70. Cached input is discounted by 95 percent, and the model runs at about 100 tokens a second. StepFun reports 67.7 on DeepSWE v1.1, against 74.1 for GPT-6 Astra in its own table, and an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 44.

Those numbers are StepFun's. One account says Artificial Analysis rates it at about the same intelligence as Kimi K3 Max at around 65 percent lower task cost. The company claims a per-task cost one-eighth that of Claude Opus 5. We have not seen an independent Artificial Analysis post on the model, and the material does not include the prices behind the comparison.

It is the company's first major release in almost two years, according to one developer. He says the model appeared quietly on the platform last week before Sunday's announcement. StepFun said through the day that demand was much higher than expected and that it was working on capacity. TestingCatalog noted the release the same morning.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse gets its first television ad as reviewers question its data habits
stories.standfirst: Alexandr Wang says the spot runs nationwide this weekend, while WIRED reports the app opts users into training-data collection and asks for bank and passport details.
body: Meta's Muse assistant aired its first national television advertisement this weekend, Alexandr Wang of Meta said on Saturday, adding that it would run during the weekend's big games. One market commentator posted the spot on Sunday, saying Meta had just aired it. Wang said the reception has been beyond the team's biggest dreams.

The ad follows a week of releases. Muse's account listed Muse for Mac, expansion to Canada on iOS and web with Android to follow, connectors with Granola and Notion, and a developer platform. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the Mac version can work with a user's files and apps to take action on their behalf. Wang also promoted a Muse Spark 1.3 coding model for use in OpenCode.

The reviews are less warm. WIRED reported on Sunday that the app continues Meta's trend of opting users into data collection for AI training, and that it nudges users to share bank account, email and passport information. The Verge wrote on Saturday that Muse probably cannot see a user's notifications, but also has no idea how it itself works.

The economics are unexplained. One analyst notes that Meta appears to give each user a cloud virtual machine with CPUs, 8GB of memory and 7.5GB of disk, and asks where the product will be monetised. Meta has not said. Axios reported on Sunday on the wider contest among OpenAI, Meta, xAI and Apple to build the assistant people use.

stories.headline: Anthropic engineer factors RSA-896 with Claude and 2,048 idle GPUs
stories.standfirst: Steve Weis says the model ported a decades-old sieve to GPUs and ran it for ten days, with no new mathematics and no threat to keys in use.
body: Steve Weis, an engineer at Anthropic, published a 135-digit factor of RSA-896 on Saturday, a 270-digit challenge number from the RSA Factoring Challenge list of 1991. His write-up says Claude ported CADO-NFS, an open-source implementation of the number field sieve, to GPUs, and that the run used about 30 GPU-years over ten days on up to 2,048 GPUs.

Weis was explicit about what it does not mean. There were no algorithmic improvements, factoring remains subexponential in the key size, and there is no new threat to deployed keys, he wrote. Deployed RSA-2048 keys are about a billion times harder than RSA-1024, which is itself roughly 30 times harder than RSA-896, according to one cryptography commentator.

The compute was scavenged. Weis said the job ran at the lowest priority on GPUs Anthropic already owned, in gaps between real work, and that the main engineering difficulty was constant pre-emption and recovery. He said he did not intervene: the model fixed discovered bugs such as out-of-memory errors on its own.

It is the third record in sixteen days. Andrew Curran noted that the public factoring record moved from 829 bits to 862 and now 896, each with AI assistance. Cognition's Devin agents took RSA-260 earlier this month. Weis said he had been working on RSA-260 when Cognition beat him to it, using the same approach. One reader verified that the published factor multiplies out to the full modulus.

stories.headline: Mathematicians doubt report that OpenAI is close to the Hodge conjecture
stories.standfirst: The Information cited a person with knowledge of the work. Elliot Glazer says progress on a special case is likely, and a full solution this month is not.
body: OpenAI is close to solving the Hodge conjecture, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, The Information reported on Saturday, citing a person with knowledge of the work. The claim follows an Odd Lots interview in which Greg Brockman acknowledged significant progress on another such problem after the Navier-Stokes work. He did not say which problem.

Elliot Glazer, who has offered public wagers on the question, disputed the report's reach on Sunday. His view is that OpenAI may have made significant progress on a special case, Hodge for abelian varieties. That gives little reason to expect a full solution soon, he says. He put his confidence that a Millennium problem falls this month at 1 percent, down from 10.

Glazer said the report's source added two things to the public record. The problem is Hodge, and the lab is close to the full result. He strongly doubts the second. OpenAI would not leak progress over weeks if its team thought the full result was in reach, he argued, given the risk of Anthropic scooping it.

Another poster, Obhishek Saha, wrote that there is no chance OpenAI has proved the conjecture in general. A proof for all abelian varieties would still count among the best results produced by language models so far, he added. Prediction markets put the odds of a Millennium problem falling this year at 58 percent, according to one account.

stories.headline: xAI's Grok Imagine Image 2.0 climbs to fourth on Artificial Analysis
stories.standfirst: The benchmark group says the model rose from 18th to 4th in text-to-image, the highest outside OpenAI, at $60 per thousand images against $211 for GPT Image 2.5.
body: Grok Imagine Image 2.0 took fourth place on the Artificial Analysis Text to Image Leaderboard, the benchmark group said on Friday. That makes it the highest ranked model outside OpenAI. The group described a 14-place climb over the previous generation, from 18th to 4th in text to image and from 16th to 10th in image editing. It placed the model on the Pareto frontier for quality against price.

The model was released in August, according to Artificial Analysis. It supports text to image, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to five input images. The group said the model closed the gap to the leaders on every text-to-image capability and use case it measures. Editing was strongest in animation and gaming, live-action film, and knowledge work.

Posts on Sunday put the Elo score at 1,154 and the price at $60 per thousand images, against about $211 for GPT Image 2.5. The leaderboard is built from votes in the group's Image Arena rather than from a fixed test, so the Elo figure measures preference. The price comparison comes from a follower rather than from Artificial Analysis.

xAI has shipped elsewhere too. Artificial Analysis said on Friday that Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 took first place on its streaming transcription benchmark, at 2.7 percent word error rate and $0.20 an hour. Followers said they had expected Grok 4.7 instead. That model has not appeared.
